chunks: "The capacitor still holds its charge, but it can't deliver it fast enough.
The connection between the capacitor and the chip is inductance, so when the chip's current steps in a nanosecond, the pin voltage dips by L times di/dt before the capacitor can respond.
A 100 milliamp step in a nanosecond across 1 nanohenry is 100 millivolts; across 10 nanohenries, which is what a centimetre or so of trace and vias gives you, it's a full volt.
That shows up as supply glitches right at the pin.

What you see in hardware: random resets or brown-out triggers, logic errors or corrupted bits when many outputs switch together, noise or offset on ADC readings, jitter on PLLs and clocks, and it fails margining, like working at 1.
The longer loop also resonates with the chip's own capacitance at a lower frequency with a higher peak, and it radiates more, so you can fail EMC scans with spurs at those frequencies.
The noise also leaks onto the shared rail, so other chips suffer. To confirm, I'd probe the supply at the pin with a spring-tip ground, not at the capacitor, and compare.

The fix is to move the capacitor closer, add smaller capacitors against the pins, put them on the back under the part with short vias, add parallel capacitors to divide the inductance, and slow the edges if I can."
